title: JSON and JSONB
subtitle: Storing and querying semi-structured data with jsonb operators and GIN indexes
author: KERNAL Team

content.text: json vs jsonb — always use jsonb

content.code:
-- json: stored as text, validated, not indexed
-- jsonb: stored as binary, can be indexed with GIN, faster to query
-- Always use jsonb unless you need to preserve key order or duplicate keys

CREATE TABLE products (
  id       BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  name     TEXT NOT NULL,
  metadata JSONB  -- dynamic attributes: color, size, material, etc.
);

INSERT INTO products (name, metadata) VALUES
  ('T-Shirt', '{"color": "red", "size": "M", "tags": ["casual", "summer"]}'),
  ('Laptop',  '{"brand": "ThinkPad", "ram_gb": 16, "storage": {"type": "SSD", "gb": 512}}');

questions.question: What is the difference between -> and ->> in PostgreSQL JSONB?
options: -> is for arrays, ->> is for objects
-> returns the value as JSON (preserves type), ->> returns it as TEXT
questions.explanation: -> returns the JSON value, preserving its type (e.g., a JSON string comes back as '"red"' with quotes). ->> returns the value as a plain text string (e.g., 'red' without quotes). Use ->> when you want to compare with a text value or cast to another type: (metadata ->> 'price')::NUMERIC.

faq.q: Should I use JSONB instead of separate columns?
faq.a: Use columns for structured, frequently-queried data (email, price, status). Use JSONB for dynamic/optional attributes that vary by row (product metadata, user preferences, third-party API responses). JSONB is not a replacement for proper schema design — it is a complement for when the schema needs to be flexible.

examples: Shopify stores product options (size, color, material) in a JSONB column since different product types have different attributes
Logging and audit trails often use JSONB to store the full 'before' and 'after' state of a row change
